page: Amazon Web Services c8gb.48xlarge is a compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features 192 dedicated physical cores running on 64-bit ARMv9 AWS Graviton Neoverse-V2 processors clocked at 2.7 GHz, providing 192 vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading. Memory allocation is configured at 384.0 GB of system RAM, maintaining a 1:2 compute-optimized ratio of 2.0 GB per core. The instance provides 400 Gbps of baseline network bandwidth, contains no bundled local storage, and includes no GPU hardware accelerators.

Benchmark results demonstrate top-tier parallel compute and memory throughput capabilities. The instance scored 314,716.71 in stress-ng multi-core tests and achieved 20,128.0 in Geekbench multi-core evaluation, alongside top-tier results in Clang software compilation (87,780.0) and ray tracing (137,825.0). Large-block memory bandwidth reached 959.17 GB/sec for read and 434.92 GB/sec for write operations. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression hit 1,427.22 GB/sec, Redis SET operations reached 355.94 million operations per second, and static web serving delivered 219.73 GB/sec throughput. In contrast, single-thread performance is moderate, with stress-ng single-core (1,643.48) and Geekbench single-core (1,652.0) ranking in the middle tier. LLM prompt processing shows varying performance, ranging from 224.07 tokens/sec on 135M models to 179.14 tokens/sec on 7B models.

Hardware tradeoffs center around high core density and memory bandwidth at the expense of per-core single-thread speed and local disk availability. Because the instance lacks bundled local storage, all persistent disk storage must be provisioned externally over the network, utilizing its substantial 400 Gbps network capacity. The architecture delivers strong compute efficiency for workloads that distribute naturally across high core counts.

The c8gb.48xlarge is suitable for heavily multi-threaded workloads, including distributed build systems, large-scale software compilation, batch processing, static web serving, high-throughput in-memory data processing, and scalable microservices.
